title: How to organise cross-stitch floss
subtitle: Keeping skeins readable and tangle-free between sessions
excerpt: Organised floss is accessible floss. Skeins wound onto numbered bobbins and stored in a flat plastic case by DMC code give you any colour in seconds and prevent tangling. The system does not need to be elaborate; it needs to be consistent.
sourceNotes: Floss organisation systems documented in modern cross-stitch practice. The bobbin-and-case method is the universal standard described in all major cross-stitch guilds and publications.

glossaryTerms.definition: A small cardboard or plastic card onto which a skein of embroidery floss is wound. The thread code number is written on the bobbin. Bobbins keep skeins from tangling and allow the stitcher to find a colour by number quickly.

content.text: Cross-stitch floss arrives as loose skeins. Without a system, skeins tangle into each other between sessions, codes are lost, and finding a specific colour takes longer than stitching with it. The standard solution is the
: each skein is wound onto a numbered card and stored in a flat case with numbered slots.
Record the code before removing the label.
The paper band wrapped around a new skein carries the brand name, colour name, and thread code. Write the code onto the bobbin before you remove the band. Once the band is gone, the code is gone.
Attach one end of the skein to the notch on the bobbin.

Floss bobbins have a small notch or slot at one end. Push one end of the skein thread into the notch to anchor it, then wind the skein around the bobbin, keeping the threads tidy and under light tension.
Leave the other end free in the second notch.
Tuck the free end into the second notch so it can be pulled out for use without unspooling the whole bobbin.
Clear plastic cases with numbered slots, typically holding 25 to 50 bobbins each. Store in numerical order by thread code. Flat cases stack and take up minimal space.
A cheaper option: plastic bag dividers inserted in a ring binder, each holding several bobbins and labelled by code range. Easy to expand as the collection grows.

Small ziplock bags, one per active project, each labelled with the project name and containing only the bobbins for that chart. The colours for the current project are always at hand without searching the main collection.

Keep a printed or digital list of the colours you own with a small length of each thread taped to the list beside its code. When you run out of a colour mid-project, the list tells you exactly what to buy and the sample shows you the correct shade in the shop.
